title: Indulgences, honestly (CCC 1471–1479)
hookLine: not buying forgiveness; a release from lingering effects of sin through the Church's prayer

cards: A baseball goes through a neighbor's window. The kid knocks on the door, red in the face, and says sorry. The neighbor says, I forgive you, and means it.
The friendship is fine. But the window is still broken, and the glass is still on the floor. Forgiveness happened.
Repair hasn't yet. Hold on to that window, because today's word has a reputation, and some of what people have heard about it is wrong.

teach.h: NOT FORGIVENESS: THE GUILT IS ALREADY GONE.
teach.b: First, what an indulgence is not. It is not forgiveness of sin. The Catechism says it only touches sins whose guilt is already forgiven; the apology and the pardon come first, in confession.
So what's left? Catholic teaching says sin has two kinds of consequence. One is the break with God, which forgiveness heals.
The other it calls temporal punishment: the leftover damage, the bent habits, the attachments that still pull. The glass on the floor. That needs healing, here or, Catholics believe, in purgatory.
An indulgence, the Catechism says, is a release from some or all of it, through the Church: partial, or plenary, which means full. Second, where it comes from. Not from a person's effort alone.

teach.h: THE COMMUNION OF SAINTS, A TREASURY.
teach.b: The Catechism points to the communion of saints: all God's people, living and dead, bound together, so the holiness of one helps the others.
It calls this the Church's treasury: the merits of Christ, and the prayers and good works of Mary and the saints.

The Church opens it for a person, attached to a prayer, a pilgrimage or a work of mercy, done with a turned heart. Catholics can also offer an indulgence for someone who has died. Third, the honest part.

There were times when indulgences were preached for money, and that abuse became one of the sparks of the Reformation. Martin Luther's protest began there, and Christians still read that history differently.
Catholic teaching today is plain: forgiveness was never something a person could buy. An indulgence, done rightly, asks for a changed heart, not a payment.

how: Catholics may seek an indulgence by doing a prayer or work the Church names, such as a pilgrimage or a work of mercy, together with confession, Communion and prayer for the pope's intentions, and they may offer it for someone who has died.

o: a paid pardon that wipes away a sin's guilt
release from sin's leftover effects, after forgiveness
permission ahead of time to commit a small sin

p: merits of Christ and the saints

s: the Catechism says it only touches sins whose guilt is already forgiven.
indulgences rest on the communion of saints
the holiness of one helps the others, the Church teaches.
Catholic teaching says forgiveness can be bought
forgiveness was never something a person could buy. the line: never for sale.

games.q: a friend says Catholics pay to get out of their sins. you check the Catechism. what does it say an indulgence is?
o: release from the lingering effects of sins already forgiven.
a receipt for a donation to the Church.
games.why: the guilt is forgiven first. an indulgence touches what's left over, through the Church's prayer and the communion of saints.

practice: Think of something you've been forgiven for, by a friend, a parent, a partner, or, if you pray, by God, and then notice what's still on the floor: a habit that keeps pulling, trust still mending, a sharpness you still reach for.
Don't scold yourself; just name one piece of glass. If you pray, ask for help with that repair; if you don't, simply notice that being forgiven and being healed can be two different moments.

wordCard.voice: Indulgence. In Catholic teaching, a release, through the Church's prayer and the communion of saints, from the lingering effects of sins already forgiven. Not forgiveness itself, and not for sale. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: never for sale. Forgiven first, repaired after. Go gently, and come back tomorrow.
